_about: News page. Add new items at the top of items. verified=true only after someone opened the DOI/URL and checked who, venue, date and every number in gist/plain/tech. Fields: gist (one line), plain (a short story for anyone), tech (for specialists), borrow (what this project takes from it or tests), status (planned, running, done, or context for background items with no test of ours). url is a https://doi.org/ link. topic: one of the names in topics (add a new topic only when five or more items need it). field_now: a short summary of where the field stands (fronts with library ids from docs/library/library.json).

landscape.method: Counts are estimates from keyword matches in OpenAlex titles and abstracts, journal articles and reviews only, for the 12 months to the update date. A paper can match more than one direction, and the headline removes people counted twice. Distinct authors and institutions are exact up to 400 papers per direction and extrapolated from the newest 400 above that. Each direction lists its exact query so anyone can check it.
landscape.headline: Roughly 4,100 researchers published journal papers on how life began in the past year, across these 10 directions.

directions.name: Prebiotic chemistry
directions.bet: Find plausible reactions on the early Earth that make life's building blocks: nucleotides, amino acids, lipids.

query.search: ("prebiotic chemistry" OR "prebiotic synthesis" OR "prebiotically plausible" OR "prebiotic conditions" OR "origin of life" OR "origins of life") AND (synthesis OR reaction OR nucleotide OR "amino acid" OR peptide OR phosphorylation)

directions.now: Cyanosulfidic chemistry keeps adding steps, such as phosphate activation and protecting groups. Wet-dry and heat-flow setups test where those steps could run.
directions.us: Our pathway map found no route that stays continuous under our sealed step-compatibility rule.

directions.name: Organics from space
directions.bet: Asteroid samples (Bennu, Ryugu) and meteorites show which building blocks space delivered to the young Earth.

query.search: (Bennu OR Ryugu OR "carbonaceous chondrite" OR "carbonaceous chondrites" OR meteorite OR meteorites OR cometary) AND ("amino acids" OR nucleobases OR organics OR "organic matter" OR prebiotic)

directions.now: Samples returned from Ryugu and Bennu now show all five nucleobases, sugars, ammonia and brines, and comets look less likely as a source of cyanide. Large mission teams inflate the author count here.

directions.name: Origins and life detection beyond Earth
directions.bet: Origin-of-life theory guides where to look for life elsewhere and how to tell it from chemistry.

query.search: (astrobiology OR biosignature OR biosignatures OR "life detection" OR "agnostic biosignature") AND ("origin of life" OR "origins of life" OR abiogenesis OR prebiotic OR habitability)

directions.now: The claim of sulfur gases on K2-18 b drew rebuttals, and Mars rover teams report organic-mineral pairings at Jezero. Others are defining the abiotic background that a sign of life has to beat.

directions.name: Protocells and compartments
directions.bet: Early life needed a container: fatty-acid vesicles or droplets that grow, divide and keep their contents together.

query.search: (protocell OR protocells OR coacervate OR coacervates OR "fatty acid vesicles" OR "prebiotic compartments" OR "minimal cell") AND ("origin of life" OR "origins of life" OR prebiotic OR protocell)

directions.now: Topics include protocells that form from scratch, vesicles that grow with peptides, and protocells that mimic the shapes of early microfossils.

directions.name: Eukaryogenesis and Asgard archaea
directions.bet: Complex cells arose when an Asgard-like archaeon took in a bacterium; the Asgard genomes show how.

query.search: "Asgard archaea" OR Asgardarchaeota OR eukaryogenesis OR "origin of eukaryotes" OR "origin of the eukaryotic cell" OR "first eukaryotic common ancestor" OR "last eukaryotic common ancestor"

directions.now: Genomics of Asgard archaea keeps finding prokaryotic roots for proteins once thought to be unique to eukaryotes.

directions.name: Molecular dating and the earliest record
directions.bet: Put dates on the tree with molecular clocks calibrated by fossils and geochemical traces of the earliest life.

query.search: ("molecular clock" OR "molecular dating" OR "divergence time" OR microfossil OR microfossils OR stromatolite OR stromatolites OR "earliest life" OR "early life") AND (Archean OR Archaean OR Hadean OR Precambrian OR Paleoproterozoic OR "early Earth")

directions.now: Molecular clocks for early life are being recalibrated against the rock record, and how fossil calibrations are chosen is under scrutiny.
directions.us: Our LUCA calibration study measures how far the dates move with calibration choices.

directions.name: Metabolism first and hydrothermal settings
directions.bet: Life began as self-sustaining chemistry driven by energy gradients in vents or hot springs; genes came later.

query.search: ("hydrothermal vent" OR "hydrothermal vents" OR "alkaline vent" OR "hot spring" OR "metabolism-first" OR protometabolism OR "prebiotic metabolism" OR "geochemical") AND ("origin of life" OR "origins of life" OR prebiotic OR abiogenesis)

groups.name: Harun Tüysüz
groups.inst: Max Planck Institute for Coal Research

directions.now: Metal catalysts are driving phosphorylation and CO2 reduction under vent-like conditions, while others say the classic alkaline-vent picture needs rethinking.

directions.name: Theory: autocatalysis, assembly and information
directions.bet: General laws for how chemistry becomes life: autocatalytic networks, assembly theory, selection before genes.

query.search: ("autocatalytic set" OR "autocatalytic sets" OR "autocatalytic network" OR "autocatalytic networks" OR "assembly theory" OR "assembly index" OR "chemical evolution") AND ("origin of life" OR "origins of life" OR abiogenesis OR prebiotic)

directions.now: Assembly theory is under heavy fire: critics say it reduces to compression. Autocatalytic-set theory is being tied to real chemistry.

directions.name: RNA world and self-copying molecules
directions.bet: Life started with RNA that both carried information and copied itself, before proteins and DNA.

query.search: "RNA world" OR "polymerase ribozyme" OR "nonenzymatic replication" OR "non-enzymatic replication" OR "nonenzymatic primer extension" OR "non-enzymatic primer extension" OR "nonenzymatic RNA copying" OR "non-enzymatic RNA copying" OR "ribozyme evolution"

directions.now: A small polymerase ribozyme that can make itself and its complementary strand (2026), and more accurate polymerases, bring self-copying RNA closer.
directions.us: Our QT45 check found net replication far below one copy per cycle, and epistasis did not predict contacts.

directions.name: LUCA and the deep tree of life
directions.bet: Rebuild the last universal common ancestor from the genes all living things share, and place the root of the tree.

query.search: "last universal common ancestor" OR "universal common ancestor" OR "root of the tree of life" OR "deep phylogeny" OR "deep phylogenomics" OR "early evolution of life"

directions.now: The 2024 reconstruction of a fairly complex LUCA, about 4.2 billion years ago, is being debated over gene-content thresholds and dating.
directions.us: Our LUCA calibration study tests how far that date moves with the choice of calibrations.

items.head: The first bacterium had a full flagellum, about twice the parts earlier counted (Selcuk et al.)
items.who: Selcuk, Andrianova, Beeby, Kearns et al.
items.gist: Sensitive searches across 80,789 genomes raise the ancestral flagellar gene set from 24 to about 50.
items.plain: Bacteria swim with a spinning tail called a flagellum, built from 40 or more parts. Earlier studies said the first bacterium had only 24 of them, implying a simpler early motor. This team searched far more genomes with more sensitive tools and found about twice as many parts were already present. Many modern bacteria have since lost some parts. The lesson is that very old genes are easy to miss when they have changed a lot.
items.tech: 80,789 GTDB proteomes, relaxed HMM searches, co-presence, order-level consensus tree from 74 gene trees. 52 ancestral proteins in the June text; 49+1 = 50 in the November abstract. No probabilistic reconciliation. Shows homology-detection failure as a source of false absences at deep nodes. Dated by version 2 (posted 13 Nov 2026); version 1 was posted in June.
items.borrow: For #32 we add a homology-search failure step to the simulated pipeline, since missed divergent homologs push deep-node presence down before reconciliation even starts.
items.topic: LUCA and the tree of life

items.head: A single mirror-image letter stops RNA copying cold (Essex, Jia, Zhang and Szostak)
items.who: Essex, Jia, Zhang, Szostak
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society
items.gist: In modern nonenzymatic RNA copying, an L-nucleotide at the end of a growing strand blocks any further extension.
items.plain: Life's RNA uses only one mirror form of its sugars. Early chemistry would have made both. This study tested what the wrong-handed letters do to RNA copying without enzymes. Mixed pairs still bind the template but react slowly, which slows copying. Worse, once a wrong-handed letter is added to the end, copying stops, because its reactive group points the wrong way. Sorting out handedness must have come before copying.
items.tech: Abstract only. 2-aminoimidazole-activated D and L nucleotides form heterochiral imidazolium-bridged dinucleotides slightly faster than homochiral ones; heterochiral bridges bind D-RNA primer-template complexes well but react slowly (competitive inhibition); L/L bridges show higher Km and much slower extension. Crystal structures: L-nucleotides base-pair normally but the reactive phosphate is misoriented; a 3'-terminal L-nucleotide is a chain terminator.
items.borrow: Our step tables (#4/#5) should list near-homochiral activated nucleotides as an input to the copying step, so the chirality hand-off is scored as a gap.

items.head: Comets probably did not deliver concentrated cyanide to early Earth (Anslow et al.)
items.who: Anslow, McDonald, Bonsor, Rimmer et al.
items.gist: Best-case simulations give a median of zero comet impacts that left 10 mM HCN on land.
items.plain: Many origin-of-life recipes start with concentrated hydrogen cyanide, and comets carry a lot of it, so comets are often named as the supplier. This study simulated early Earth's comet bombardment a hundred thousand times, letting comets break up in the air, heat up on impact and land only on the little dry land there was. In most runs, not a single comet left enough cyanide in one place. Mars, with a thin atmosphere and slower impacts, would have done far better.
items.tech: 10^5 Monte Carlo runs; median successful (>10 mM HCN on land) impacts = 0; 54% of runs had none; most likely timing 4.41 (+0.11/-0.29) Gya; fewer than 5% of runs had a success after 4.03 Gya. Without land limits: Mars 744 ± 27, Earth 87 ± 9, Venus 24 ± 5. All poorly known inputs were set to favour delivery. Caveats: HCN survival model ignores strength and porosity; long-period comets excluded; other feedstocks assumed to be worse.
items.borrow: Removes or downgrades cometary HCN as a feedstock source in the pond and cyanosulfidic step tables (#5/#17/#20); local feedstock must come from atmospheric or crustal sources instead.

items.head: A polymerase ribozyme now copies RNA with 94% accuracy per letter (Horning, Nasser and Joyce)
items.who: Horning, Nasser, Joyce
items.gist: Thirty-three rounds of evolution made an RNA enzyme that copies RNA more accurately and copies harder templates.
items.plain: An RNA world needs an RNA molecule that can copy RNA. Lab-evolved polymerase ribozymes can already make long strands, but they make many mistakes and stall on folded templates. This team ran 33 more rounds of selection. Accuracy rose from 86% to 94% per letter, and the enzyme copied templates it used to fail on. It still cannot copy itself.
items.tech: Preprint (abstract only). Fidelity measured while synthesizing the class I ligase ribozyme: 86% to 94% per nucleotide, from fewer misincorporations and less extension of mismatched termini. Broader template generality, including highly structured templates. At 94% per nucleotide the expected error-free length is short, so replication of a polymerase-length RNA remains out of reach.
items.borrow: A comparison row for our QT45 net-replication result (#2/#18). It does not change that verdict, which rests on yield per cycle and strand decay rather than accuracy.

items.head: Side reactions do not automatically doom early metabolic cycles (Peng, Spencer, Baum)
items.who: Peng, Spencer, Baum
items.venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface
items.gist: Once reactions are treated as reversible in an open system, side products can act as a backup store of the cycle's own molecules.
items.plain: A classic objection to metabolism-first origins says that without enzymes, side reactions would drain a self-copying chemical cycle until it dies. This team worked through the math for the simplest cycles in a fed, flowing reactor. If a side reaction is truly one-way, it always hurts. But real reactions run both ways, and then the side product can turn back into the cycle's molecule. Depending on rates, the side reaction can hurt, do nothing, or even help.
items.tech: CSTR with A + F <-> 2A and A <-> B. Irreversible side reaction: survival needs k1 > k3 + kd/f and always lowers [A]. Fully reversible: sign of U(k1..k4, kd, f) can be either way; stochastic runs show harmful-then-beneficial cases. Extended algebraically to a two-step cycle with three side reactions. Toy networks only.
items.borrow: Bears on our RAF tasks #6/#8/#23: adds a dynamic persistence check that graph-only RAF detection lacks.

items.head: Lifeless protocells pass common tests for ancient microfossils (Gillet de Chalonge et al.)
items.who: Gillet de Chalonge, Field, Dignam, Coutant et al.
items.gist: Abiotic protocells made under vent-like conditions look like early microfossils and even get labeled bacterial or archaeal by an FTIR index.
items.plain: Claims of the oldest fossils rest on shape and chemistry thought to be unique to life. This team made simple protocells from basic organic molecules in warm, alkaline, silica-rich water like a hydrothermal setting. They formed spheres, threads and lens shapes that look like supposed Archaean microfossils. Their infrared spectra overlapped with real microbes, and a common index even sorted them into bacteria, archaea or eukaryotes. The authors argue current fossil tests can be fooled.
items.tech: (abstract only) Low-temperature alkaline hydrothermal synthesis with silica; FTIR spectra overlap; R3/2 ratio classifies eight protocell systems as bacterial, archaeal or eukaryotic. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
items.borrow: Strengthens our rule for #22: any life-detection metric needs abiotic look-alike controls, not just meteorites.

items.head: Impact model puts the RNA World's best window at about 4.33 billion years ago (Abramov et al.)
items.who: Abramov, Medvegy, Kremer, Mojzsis
items.gist: A 3-D model of Hadean impacts finds the crust stopped being sterilized about 4.4 billion years ago, with a sweet spot for RNA chemistry near 4.33.
items.plain: The young Earth was pounded by asteroids that heated its crust. This team simulated that heating across the whole planet and checked it against the oldest zircon crystals. Before about 4.4 billion years ago, impacts kept wiping out any fragile molecules. After that, cooler pockets and hot springs persisted, peaking around 4.33 billion years ago, a bit before most estimates of the last universal common ancestor.
items.tech: 3-D thermal bombardment model, 0.13-0.57 wt% delivered mass, zircon benchmark. Sterilization until about 4.4 Ga; biocompatible near-surface volume > 90% by 4.3 Ga; sweet spot 4.33 Ga (shifts to about 4.4 Ga at 0.13 wt%). Sensitive to the assumed delivered mass.
items.borrow: Context only: it sets the geological clock that LUCA-size arguments are measured against.

items.head: Alkaline vent theories rest on conditions ancient vents may not have had (Tutolo)
items.who: Tutolo
items.gist: A geochemist argues early Lost City-type vents lacked hot pH gradients, sulfide and an easy path to complex hydrocarbons.
items.plain: A popular idea puts life's start at alkaline seafloor vents, where natural proton gradients across iron-sulfur walls could power the first cells. This review argues the ancient versions of these vents were shallower and shorter-lived. Lost City fluids only become very alkaline after they cool, so there is no strong gradient where it is hot. Early oceans had little sulfur, so iron-sulfur walls would be rare. And making long carbon chains for membranes looks too slow at those temperatures.
items.tech: (abstract only) Four lines: shallower and less focused ancient serpentinizing circulation; hyperalkalinity only after cooling; near-absent sulfide given sulfate- and sulfide-poor oceans and S-poor serpentinites; kinetic barriers to complex hydrocarbon formation seen at Lost City and in the lab. Also questions vent-based habitability arguments for Mars, icy moons and exoplanets.
items.borrow: Affects our vent route step table (#4/#5): we plan a scored variant with gradient-, sulfide- and hydrocarbon-dependent steps failing. Sealed test: before rescoring, record the predicted change in route success under the Tutolo variant.

items.head: First 3D structures of RNA polymerase ribozymes show how they grip their templates (Szokoli et al.; Strutzenberg et al.)
items.who: Szokoli et al.; Strutzenberg, Horning, Joyce, Lyumkis et al.
items.gist: Two cryo-EM studies reveal how lab-evolved RNA copiers are built, and one structure already led to a faster enzyme.
items.plain: The best lab models of an RNA world copier were evolved for years without anyone seeing their shape. Two groups have now imaged them. One structure shows a hidden pairing that ties up the end the enzyme needs, and breaking it made the enzyme faster. The other shows the enzyme holding template, primer and incoming letter in a 'right hand' shape like protein polymerases. Structure can now guide design.
items.tech: Preprints (abstracts only). Szokoli et al.: substrate-free tC19Z at 3.1 Å; accessory domain contacts the ancestral class I ligase via a loop-loop contact, a Mg2+ seam and a six-base stack; an ectopic pairing sequesters the 5' end, and compensatory mutations raise extension rate. Strutzenberg et al. (doi:10.64898/2026.08.30.748161, Joyce and Lyumkis labs): polymerase bound to template, primer and an NTP analog; modular flanking elements around a conserved ligase core, arranged like the 'right hand' of protein polymerases.
items.borrow: Gives our QT45 contact test (#30, negative) a positive control: check whether epistasis-based contact prediction recovers contacts in a solved polymerase before trusting it on QT45.

items.head: Better reconciliation models put the archaeal root at Euryarchaeota and make the first archaeon a methanogen (Huang et al.)
items.who: Huang, Dombrowski, Mahendrarajah, Wahl et al.
items.gist: Letting gene gain and loss rates vary by lineage moved the archaeal root away from small-genome symbionts and gave a 1.6 to 2.1 Mb thermophilic methanogen ancestor.
items.plain: Archaea are one of the two great branches of microbial life, and nobody agrees where their family tree starts. Some trees put tiny parasitic archaea at the base, which would mean the first archaeon was small and simple. This team counted how genes were copied, lost and passed sideways across 257 genomes, and let those rates differ between groups. Tiny parasites lose genes fast; once the model allowed that, the root moved to the methane-making Euryarchaeota. The reconstructed ancestor was a heat-loving methane maker with roughly 800 to 1,700 gene families.
items.tech: AleRax v1.1.1, 7,059 arCOG families, 1,000 bootstrap trees each, 257 genomes. BIC-selected 72-parameter branch-wise DTL model; AU tests leave only the Euryarchaeota and MHH roots. DPANN loss rate 0.40-0.45 vs 0.26-0.27 elsewhere; a global model gives a small-genome-attraction root. LACA 1.58 Mb (Euryarchaeota root) or 2.06 Mb (MHH root); 800-1,219 or 1,190-1,709 families from PP thresholds 0.5 and 0.75. No simulation test of root-content recovery is reported in the main text; no false-negative correction. Data and reconciliations on Zenodo 18701544.
items.borrow: Feeds #32 directly: we add lineage-varying loss rates to the Zombi truth model, and we can apply the calibration to their LACA per-family PPs as a second target. A sealed test fits naturally: predict the calibrated LACA family count from our LUCA-depth calibration before running it on their PPs.
items.topic: LUCA and the tree of life

items.head: Assembly index can be estimated from simple mass spectra, but the life test is still untested (Rutter et al.)
items.who: Rutter, Sharma, Seet, Obeh Alobo et al.
items.gist: A machine-learning model predicts a molecule's assembly index from flight-style mass spectra; no living vs non-living samples were compared.
items.plain: Assembly theory scores a molecule by the fewest joining steps needed to build it. The Cronin group trained a model to guess that score from the kind of simple mass spectrum a Titan or Europa probe would record. The guesses were about three times closer than a curve fitted to molecular weight. But the paper never measured samples from living and non-living sources, so it does not show that the score detects life. Its own database comparison found that, at equal size, catalogued lab molecules score higher than natural products.
items.tech: XGBoost on vectorized NIST SRD 69 EI MS1 spectra (n = 32,603 molecules, 70/30 split). Relative MSE 0.04 vs 0.12 for the best baseline; 0.07 on MassBank EI-B vs 0.12 for a molecular-weight power law. CFM-ID simulated MS2 at fixed energy gives about 0.03; mixing energies hurts. MA scales with bond count with exponent 0.74 (R2 0.74). At matched bond count PubChem > COCONUT 2.0 in MA. Data: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20586263.
items.borrow: Feeds #22 (red-team) and #7 (AI vs size null): we can rerun a size-matched natural-product vs PubChem comparison on their data. A sealed test: predict before looking that COCONUT mean MA is below PubChem mean MA at every bond count from 10 to 40.

items.head: LUCA's enzyme set was incomplete; metals and phosphite may have filled the gaps (Mrnjavac et al.)
items.who: Mrnjavac, Hoffmann, Schlikker, Burmeister et al.
items.gist: Of the core metabolic enzymes, 166 trace to LUCA while 127 were added later in the bacterial or archaeal lines, and nickel and palladium make ADP from phosphite in water.
items.plain: This team asked which enzymes of core metabolism were already in the last universal common ancestor. Many amino acid and vitamin-making enzymes appear only after bacteria and archaea split, so LUCA's own enzyme kit had gaps. They propose that metals found at hydrothermal vents did those missing jobs. In the lab, nickel and palladium helped phosphite add a phosphate to AMP, making small amounts of ADP.
items.tech: 953 genomes, MCL clusters mapped to 424 core reactions. LUCA = present in >= 50% of genomes of >= 4 higher taxa in both domains (no reconciliation). 166 LUCA, 89 LBCA-lineage, 38 LACA-lineage, 37 unassigned. Ni0 gave 6.74 uM ADP from 100 mM AMP. Caveat: an occupancy rule cannot tell early transfer from inheritance.
items.borrow: For #32 we use their occupancy rule as a baseline classifier in the simulations; for #28 and #23 their enzyme-age table is a second labelling to test.
items.topic: LUCA and the tree of life

items.head: Early Earth's own volcanic rocks could have supplied reactive phosphorus (Baidya et al.)
items.who: Baidya, Walton, Kalita, Szilas et al.
items.gist: Common lava and mantle rocks carry phosphite and pyrophosphate that weathering could release.
items.plain: Life needs phosphorus, but the usual form, phosphate, is hard to dissolve and slow to react. Chemists prefer phosphite and pyrophosphate, which are more soluble and reactive, but it was unclear where early Earth got them besides rare meteorite pieces. This team measured rocks like basalt and komatiite from 15 places and found that on average about 5% and up to 24% of the phosphorus in ultramafic rocks is phosphite. A simple model says a shaded volcanic lake could build up tens of micromolar phosphite, while the open ocean would stay far lower.
items.tech: Phosphite up to 7%, 24%, 17%, 0.6% of total P in olivine, peridotite, komatiite, basalt; pyrophosphate up to 5% (komatiite) and 0.4% (basalt). Oceanic crust 3.5 to 2.0 Ga: 4 to 5 ppm each. Deep ocean box model: up to 1 nM with UV oxidation, 1 to 2 µM if photo-oxidation is suppressed (abstract says up to 1 µM). Lake: up to 67 µM UV-shielded, below 0.1 µM exposed. Caveats: simple box models, no pyrophosphate model, no test that these levels drive phosphorylation.
items.borrow: Feeds the phosphorus supply rows of the pond and vent step tables (#4/#5/#20). A sealed test is possible: before scoring, write down whether the 67 µM shielded-lake ceiling clears each downstream phosphorylation step's stated concentration, then score.

items.head: First sugar found in interstellar space: erythrulose (Jiménez-Serra et al.)
items.who: Jiménez-Serra, García de la Concepción, Cuppen, Rey-Montejo et al.
items.gist: A four-carbon sugar shows up in a Galactic Centre gas cloud, more common than smaller sugars.
items.plain: Sugars like ribose have been found in meteorites and in samples from asteroid Bennu, but no sugar had ever been seen in the gas between stars. Using two radio telescopes, this team found erythrulose, a four-carbon sugar, in a cloud near the centre of our galaxy. Oddly, smaller three-carbon sugars were not seen at all. Computer models suggest erythrulose forms on icy dust from two common smaller molecules, so sugars might be made before planets form.
items.tech: G+0.693-0.027; 12 line sets (17 transitions), p6 = 0.2% chance alignment; N = (8.7 ± 0.8) x 10^13 cm^-2, abundance (6.4 ± 0.6) x 10^-10; C3 sugars ≤4 x 10^-11 and ≤7 x 10^-11, so erythrulose is ≥8 to 17 times more abundant. Proposed route: glycolaldehyde radical plus ethylene glycol radical on ice, both enantiomers 50% each. Ice models within a factor of 5 for erythrulose but overproduce C3 sugars by about 25 to 70. Delivery estimate about (0.5 to 50) x 10^9 kg. Caveat: one source, crowded spectrum.
items.borrow: Adds an exogenous C4 sugar feedstock option to the pathway map (ice-RNA and pond routes). It does not touch our sealed Bennu/Ryugu nucleobase and ammonia predictions directly.

items.head: Critics say assembly theory reduces to dictionary compression (Ozelim, Uthamacumaran, Abrahão et al.)
items.who: Ozelim, Uthamacumaran, Abrahão, Hernández-Orozco et al.
items.gist: The latest round of the assembly-theory dispute: critics say the 2025 defence used incomplete controls.
items.plain: Assembly theory proposes a number, the assembly index, that counts how many joining steps a molecule needs; its authors say high values in large amounts mean life. In 2025 they argued the index is not just a file-compression score. This reply reruns and extends their examples and says that, once proper comparisons are added, the index behaves like ordinary dictionary compression and adds nothing new.
items.tech: Reply to Kempes et al. 2025 (npj Complexity 2:27, doi:10.1038/s44260-025-00049-9), which argued the assembly index sits in a different computational complexity class from Shannon entropy, Huffman and LZW. Ozelim et al. say the defence's experiments are incomplete as controls, that extended versions overlap with dictionary-based statistical compression, and restate their earlier claim of equivalence to the Shannon entropy rate (Abrahão et al. 2024, PLOS Complex Systems, doi:10.1371/journal.pcsy.0000014). Earlier rounds: Hazen et al. 2024 (minerals up to index 21) and the Walker et al. 2024 reply (doi:10.1098/rsif.2024.0367).
items.borrow: Both sides argue in theory. Our task #7 settles one part with data: does assembly index separate biotic from abiotic mass-spec samples better than molecular weight or LZ complexity alone?

items.head: Phenotype predictors trained on deliberately noisy genomes read traits back to the first bacterium (Koldaeva et al.)
items.who: Koldaeva, Bagrova, Mitchell, Hugenholtz et al.
items.gist: Adding fake gene losses and gains during training lets models predict oxygen use and cell envelope for reconstructed ancestral genomes at the bacterial root.
items.plain: Reconstructed ancestral genomes are blurry: some genes are missed and some are wrongly added. This team trained computer models to guess traits like oxygen use from gene lists, and during training they blurred the lists on purpose. The blurred-trained models kept working on uncertain ancestral genomes. They predict the first bacterium lived without oxygen, had two membranes and liked warm water, roughly 46 to 75 C.
items.tech: XGBoost on COG copy numbers, taxonomy-aware holdouts. Noise: Poisson false negatives and false positives with rates drawn from uniform, exponential or gamma distributions. Ancestral expected copy numbers from reconciliation on a 1,007-taxon tree. No measured reconciliation error rates at the LBCA are given; the noise is an assumption. GC content is not recoverable at the root.
items.borrow: Context for #32: our simulations can supply measured deep-node false-negative and false-positive rates that their noise model currently assumes.
items.topic: LUCA and the tree of life

items.head: Lipid membranes made from scratch without an existing membrane (Khanal, Fracassi, Harjung, Burkart, Devaraj)
items.who: Khanal, Fracassi, Harjung, Burkart, Devaraj
items.gist: Vesicles assembled from lipids built out of acetate and cysteine, with no pre-existing membrane to grow from.
items.plain: Every cell membrane today grows from an older membrane, which raises a chicken-and-egg question for the first cell. This team built lipid tails from two simple molecules, acetate and cysteine, using enzymes dissolved in water. The new lipids assembled themselves into bubbles with two-layer walls, and some of these bubbles could hold a difference in acidity between inside and outside.
items.tech: De novo bilayer formation without pre-existing membranes, membrane proteins or lipid templates. Lipid tails are made by soluble enzymes from acetate and cysteine and form diacyl lipids that assemble into vesicles. Pore-forming peptides let precursors in, so new lipid keeps forming; glycolipid compartments maintain proton gradients. The route uses enzymes, so it is not a prebiotic pathway.
items.borrow: Evidence for the lipid-world row and the compartment step of the pathway map. Because it relies on enzymes, we score it as 'shown with biological catalysts', not as a prebiotic step.

items.head: All five nucleobases found in asteroid Ryugu (Koga, Oba, Takano, Naraoka et al.)
items.who: Koga, Oba, Takano, Naraoka et al.
items.gist: Ryugu, like Bennu, holds all five letters used in DNA and RNA.
items.plain: Japan's Hayabusa2 brought back grains of asteroid Ryugu. Uracil was found in them in 2023; this study now reports all five nucleobases, the 'letters' of DNA and RNA. Ryugu has roughly equal amounts of the two families of bases, unlike Bennu and the Orgueil meteorite, which lean one way. The balance tracks how much ammonia each body had, which hints that the bases formed by one shared chemistry under different local conditions.
items.tech: Adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil in Ryugu samples. Purines and pyrimidines are near equal in Ryugu; Murchison is purine-rich; Bennu and Orgueil pyrimidine-rich. Across Ryugu, Bennu and Orgueil the purine-to-pyrimidine ratio correlates negatively with ammonia.
items.borrow: A ratio-versus-ammonia trend is exactly the kind of relationship task #11 can extend into a sealed prediction for compounds not yet reported from returned samples.

items.head: A small polymerase ribozyme that can synthesize itself and its complementary strand (Gianni, Holliger et al.)
items.who: Gianni, Kwok, Wan, Goeij, Clifton, Colizzi, Attwater, Holliger
items.gist: A 45-letter RNA, QT45, found in random sequences, copies RNA in ice and made both a copy of itself and of its partner strand.
items.plain: RNA-world ideas need an RNA that copies RNA. The known RNA copiers were large, too big to arise by chance. QT45 is only 45 letters long and was fished out of random sequences. Working in slightly alkaline ice and fed three-letter RNA pieces, it copied its partner strand and, with chosen pieces, itself. The yields are tiny, about 0.2% after 72 days, but the find suggests such copiers may be less rare than thought.
items.tech: QT45 (45 nt) from random pools catalyses general RNA-templated RNA synthesis from trinucleotide triphosphates in mildly alkaline eutectic ice. Complementary-strand synthesis with a random triplet pool at 94.1% per-nucleotide fidelity; self-synthesis with defined substrates; both ~0.2% yield in 72 days. Triplets are pre-activated and supplied. Online 12 Feb 2026, issue dated March 2026.
items.borrow: The closest result to the step from template copying (L2) to self-replication (L3). Task #2 extracts its numbers; task #12 seals a prediction for its untested double mutants. The founding plan's second-hand '0.02% over 72 days' was wrong; the paper says about 0.2%.

items.head: Bio-essential sugars, including ribose, in samples from asteroid Bennu (Furukawa et al.)
items.who: Furukawa, Sunami, Takano, Koga et al.
items.gist: Ribose, the sugar in RNA, and glucose found in Bennu; deoxyribose, the DNA sugar, was not.
items.plain: With ribose found, every part of RNA has now been detected in Bennu's returned grains. The team also found glucose, the most plentiful sugar in the sample, and several other sugars. They did not find deoxyribose, the sugar in DNA. That fits the idea that RNA came before DNA, though it does not prove it.
items.tech: Ribose 0.097 ± 0.014 nmol/g, lyxose 0.018 ± 0.007, arabinose 0.11 ± 0.03, xylose 0.079 ± 0.033, glucose 0.35 ± 0.05, galactose 0.014 ± 0.004 nmol/g. Total sugars 0.668 nmol/g, about 1 mol% of Bennu amino acids. 2-Deoxyribose not found. Online 2 Dec 2025, issue January 2026.
items.borrow: Supports an RNA-first chemistry. Sugar ratios feed the Bennu abundance prediction (task #11).

items.head: Thioester-mediated RNA aminoacylation and peptidyl-RNA synthesis in water (Singh, Powner et al.)
items.who: Singh, Thoma, Whitaker, Satterly Webley, Yao, Powner
items.gist: Amino acids carried on sulfur compounds attach to the ends of RNA in water, ahead of joining to each other.
items.plain: Cells make proteins by first loading amino acids onto transfer RNAs, a job done by enzymes. This study shows a chemical way to do the loading without enzymes: amino acids bound to thiols, sulfur compounds still used by cells, stick to the right spot on RNA rather than linking up into random chains. Several prebiotic starting materials make these thiol compounds in water.
items.tech: Aminoacyl-thiols react selectively with RNA 2',3'-diols over amines, so aminoacylation beats non-coded peptide bonding; scope covers 14 proteinogenic amino acids. Prebiotic nitriles, N-carboxyanhydrides and amino-acid anhydrides react with thiols (including CoA and coenzyme M) to give aminoacyl-thiols. Switching to thioacid activation favours peptides; one-pot peptidyl-RNA at neutral pH.
items.borrow: A concrete step toward linking amino acids to RNA, which coding needs. It enters the pathway map as the activation step, with its conditions recorded.

items.head: Insufficient evidence for DMS and DMDS in the atmosphere of K2-18 b (Luque et al.)
items.who: Luque, Piaulet-Ghorayeb, Radica, Xue, Zhang, Bean, Samra, Steinrueck
items.gist: No statistically significant detection of DMS or DMDS when all JWST data on K2-18 b are analysed together.
items.plain: A 2025 claim said JWST had seen a gas on the planet K2-18 b that on Earth comes only from life. This team analysed all three JWST instruments' data together, using several processing pipelines and two retrieval codes. The evidence for the gas was not significant, and other simple molecules fit the data as well.
items.tech: Joint 0.6-12 µm NIRISS, NIRSpec and MIRI analysis with three reductions and two retrieval codes. No statistically significant evidence for DMS or DMDS; methyl-bearing molecules such as ethane fit as well. With the best-fitting DMS/DMDS model, about 25 more MIRI transits are needed for a 3-sigma rejection of a flat line. arXiv:2505.13407.
items.borrow: A reminder of how biosignature claims fail under proper alternatives. Off the origin-of-life path, so no test planned.

items.head: Carbon reduction powered by natural electrochemical gradients under vent conditions (Altair et al.)
items.who: Altair, Dragoti, Sojo, Li et al., Hudson
items.gist: A vent-wall reactor makes formic and acetic acid from CO2 and H2 using only pH gradients across iron-sulfide minerals.
items.plain: The alkaline-vent idea says the first metabolism ran on the difference in acidity between vent fluid and seawater, across thin mineral walls. This team built a bench-scale wall from iron-sulfide minerals with hydrogen-rich alkaline fluid on one side and CO2-rich acidic water on the other. Small amounts of formic and acetic acid, the first two steps of an ancient carbon-fixing pathway, appeared on the seawater side.
items.tech: FeS, Ni-FeS and FeS2 barriers produced micromolar formic and acetic acid on the ocean side (pH 5.7, CO2) against an H2, pH 11 vent side; e.g. FeS2 at 25 °C gave 4.2 µM formic and 2.5 µM acetic acid after 24 h, none on the vent side. Currents of 10 nA to 10 µA sufficed. At 75 °C on both sides Ni-FeS gave about 816 µM formic acid. Builds on Hudson et al. 2020 (PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.2002659117).
items.borrow: Vent step tables (task #4) record these yields with their conditions. Products still stop at two carbons.

items.head: High-yield polymerisation of cyclic nucleotides under wet-dry cycling (Caimi, Braun, Fraccia et al.)
items.who: Caimi, Langlais, Fontana, Wunnava, Bellini, Braun, Fraccia
items.gist: Repeated drying and wetting joins all four RNA letters into short chains, with no added activating chemicals.
items.plain: Warm-pond theories say pools that dry by day and refill by night could join RNA letters into chains. Here, nucleotides in a ring-shaped form joined up on their own when only water was added each cycle, at room temperature and mildly alkaline pH. The chains were short: a few percent reached four letters and about one in a thousand reached ten.
items.tech: 2',3'-cyclic nucleotides of A, U, G and C oligomerise without external activators under wet-dry cycling. Yields reach about 70% for G and at least 20% for the others; at pH 11 polymerisation is near-balanced across the four bases with Y = 36%. Products include up to 6% 4-mers and 0.1% 10-mers; growth and hydrolysis balance after about 10 cycles.
items.borrow: First entry for the warm-pond row. The pond step table records that wet-dry cycling gives short mixed oligomers; the gap to copyable lengths is named.

items.head: Triplet substrates under pH and freeze-thaw cycles enable exponential RNA replication by a ribozyme (Attwater, Holliger et al.)
items.who: Attwater, Augustin, Curran, Kwok, Ohlendorf, Gianni, Holliger
items.gist: An RNA enzyme replicated both strands of short double-stranded RNAs exponentially, including a piece of itself.
items.plain: Copied RNA strands stick to their templates so tightly that copying stalls. This team found that the three-letter RNA pieces used as building blocks also hold the separated strands apart. Combined with cycles of freezing, thawing and acidity changes, an RNA polymerase ribozyme could replicate both strands of short RNAs over and over, including a fragment of the ribozyme itself. Started from random RNA, the system produced either a few winning replicators or slowly drifting mixtures.
items.tech: Triplets bind and kinetically trap dissociated strands while serving as substrates, overcoming the strand-separation problem. With coupled pH and freeze-thaw cycles: exponential replication of (+) and (-) strands of dsRNAs, including a ribozyme fragment. Open-ended replication of random pools yielded defined replicators or diverse pools from partial ribozyme self-replication, drifting toward hypothesised primordial codons. Substrates are supplied by the experimenter.
items.borrow: Corrects our site, which said 'no exponential growth yet' for RNA world. Ladder level L3 still needs the whole replicator copied from a setting's own feedstocks.

items.head: Abundant ammonia and nitrogen-rich organic matter in asteroid Bennu (Glavin, Dworkin et al.)
items.who: Glavin, Dworkin, Alexander, Aponte et al. (62 authors)
items.gist: 33 amino acids, 14 of the 20 used by life, and all five nucleobases in pristine Bennu samples; the chiral amino acids show no handedness bias.
items.plain: NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought back dust and pebbles from asteroid Bennu, kept away from Earth's air and life. They hold 33 amino acids, 14 of them used in proteins, all five DNA and RNA bases and lots of ammonia. Amino acids come in left- and right-handed forms; life uses only left-handed ones. The Bennu amino acids whose handedness could be measured come in equal amounts, which weakens the idea that meteorites gave Earth its bias.
items.tech: Bennu is richer in carbon, nitrogen and ammonia than Ryugu and most meteorites; 15N enrichments point to a cold outer-disc origin. 33 amino acids identified plus unidentified C6-C7 aliphatic ones; at least 23 N-heterocycles including all five canonical nucleobases; about 10,000 N-bearing species. All enantiomerically resolvable chiral non-protein amino acids (e.g. isovaline, norvaline) were racemic or near racemic, and racemic alanine and aspartic acid indicate negligible contamination.
items.borrow: Building blocks were common in the early Solar System; the racemic result counts against a meteoritic origin of life's handedness. Feeds task #11.

items.head: The nature of the last universal common ancestor and its impact on the early Earth system (Moody et al.)
items.who: Moody, Álvarez-Carretero, Mahendrarajah, Clark et al. (19 authors)
items.gist: Places LUCA about 4.2 billion years ago as a complex anaerobic acetogen living within an ecosystem.
items.plain: LUCA is the most recent ancestor shared by all living things. Using gene families that duplicated before LUCA, this team dated it to about 4.2 billion years ago, early in Earth's history. They reconstruct it as a microbe as complex as modern bacteria, living without oxygen, making acetate, and already part of a community of other organisms.
items.tech: Age about 4.2 Ga (4.09-4.33 Ga) from divergence times of pre-LUCA paralogues under cross-bracing calibration. Reconciliation suggests a genome of at least 2.5 Mb (2.49-2.99) encoding around 2,600 proteins; a prokaryote-grade anaerobic acetogen with an early immune system, embedded in an ecosystem.
items.borrow: A headline claim we re-test for robustness to its modelling choices (tasks #9 and #10). LUCA is late: it constrains the end of the origin story, not its start.
items.topic: LUCA and the tree of life

items.head: Heat flows enrich prebiotic building blocks and enhance their reactivity (Matreux, Aikkila, Scheu, Braun, Mast)
items.who: Matreux, Aikkila, Scheu, Braun, Mast
items.gist: Heat flowing through rock cracks sorts a mixed prebiotic soup, doing the purification chemists normally do by hand.
items.plain: Most origin-of-life chemistry works only because chemists purify the product of one step before the next. This team showed that warm water in thin rock cracks, heated on one side, can sort more than 50 building blocks out of a mixture. In one test the sorting boosted a reaction joining two glycines by a factor of about 100,000.
items.tech: Thermophoresis in crack-like geo-compartments separates more than 50 prebiotically relevant compounds (amino acids, nucleobases, nucleotides, polyphosphates, 2-aminoazoles) Experiments in single and three-chamber set-ups gave enrichments such as 23-fold; the up-to-three-orders-of-magnitude concentration ratios and the five-orders-of-magnitude rise in glycine dimerisation yield come from simulated 20 x 20 crack networks. Robust across crack sizes, pH, solvents and temperatures.
items.borrow: A named physical process that may stand in for a purified hand-off. The compatibility rule (task #3) must say whether such processes count.

items.head: RNA-catalysed evolution of catalytic RNA (Papastavrou, Horning, Joyce)
items.who: Papastavrou, Horning, Joyce
items.gist: An RNA polymerase ribozyme, not a protein, ran Darwinian evolution of another ribozyme, but only when its copying was accurate enough.
items.plain: Evolution needs copies that are mostly right. Here an RNA enzyme repeatedly copied a smaller RNA enzyme, and the copies that still worked were kept each round. With an older, sloppier copier the population drifted into nonsense. With an improved copier, new and fitter variants evolved. The copier itself was not evolving, so this is not yet open-ended evolution.
items.tech: A higher-fidelity polymerase replicates the hammerhead ribozyme by reciprocal synthesis of both strands, with selection for cleavage. Two parallel lineages: the low-fidelity one lost hammerhead function; the high-fidelity one evolved variants with improved fitness from mutations that raised replicability, at a small cost in activity. Deep sequencing tracked the succession.
items.borrow: The nearest result to ladder level L4. Our 'functional RNAs are common' bench uses the same kind of deep-sequencing counts.

items.head: Molecular assembly indices of mineral heteropolyanions (Hazen et al.)
items.who: Hazen, Burns, Cleaves, Downs, Krivovichev, Wong
items.gist: Some mineral building units score above the assembly-index threshold proposed for life.
items.plain: Assembly theory says molecules needing 15 or more joining steps, found in many copies, are a sign of life. This team calculated the score for clusters of atoms that form in water and build some minerals. The most complex, in the rare minerals ewingite and ilmajokite, scored 21, so a high score alone cannot mean life.
items.tech: Heteropolyanions range from assembly index 2 (H2CO3, Si(OH)4) to 21 (ewingite, ilmajokite). Reply by Walker, Mathis, Marshall and Cronin (J. R. Soc. Interface 21:20240367, 2024): the ~15 threshold comes from experimentally measured covalent organic molecules, while these indices are theoretical, from crystal structures of charged units not isolable in solution. Counter-reply: Hazen et al., 21:20240622.
items.borrow: A direct challenge to assembly index as a biosignature; task #7 tests it against a size-only classifier.

items.head: From ligase to polymerase: the class I ribozyme lineage (Bartel, Joyce and co-workers)
items.who: Johnston et al. 2001; Lincoln & Joyce 2009; Horning & Joyce 2016; Tjhung et al. 2020
items.gist: Twenty years of lab evolution turned an RNA that joins RNA into one that copies long RNAs, but not well enough to copy itself.
items.plain: In 2001 the Bartel lab evolved an RNA that could extend another RNA along a template. Joyce's lab built two RNAs that made each other and grew exponentially (2009), then evolved a polymerase that amplified RNA more than 10,000-fold in an all-RNA version of PCR (2016). By 2020 it could make its own ancestor in three pieces, but copying errors left few of those working.
items.tech: Johnston et al. 2001, Science 292:1319 (doi:10.1126/science.1060786): class I polymerase, accurate general RNA-templated primer extension. Lincoln & Joyce 2009, Science 323:1229 (doi:10.1126/science.1167856): cross-replicating ligases, self-sustained exponential amplification, doubling time about 1 h. Horning & Joyce 2016, PNAS 113:9786 (doi:10.1073/pnas.1610103113): >10,000-fold amplification of short templates. Tjhung et al. 2020, PNAS 117:2906 (doi:10.1073/pnas.1914282117): synthesises the class I ligase as three strands, most assembled ligases inactive because of copying errors.
items.borrow: The baseline for the L2 to L3 gap. The fidelity numbers set the error threshold any ribozyme model in tasks #2 and #12 must respect.

items.head: The physiology and habitat of the last universal common ancestor (Weiss et al.)
items.who: Weiss, Sousa, Mrnjavac, Neukirchen, Roettger, Nelson-Sathi, Martin
items.gist: 355 protein families point to a LUCA that lived on hydrogen, CO2 and iron, probably at a hydrothermal setting.
items.plain: This team sorted 6.1 million genes from bacteria and archaea into families and kept only 355 whose family trees reach back to the common ancestor. Those genes describe a heat-loving microbe that lived without oxygen, fed on hydrogen and CO2 and relied on iron-sulfur chemistry.
items.tech: From 286,514 protein clusters, 355 families (~0.1%) trace to LUCA by phylogenetic criteria: anaerobic, CO2-fixing, H2-dependent with a Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, N2-fixing and thermophilic, rich in FeS clusters and radical mechanisms. Clostridia and methanogens are basal.
items.borrow: One of the two gene sets our LUCA robustness scan (task #10) compares with Moody et al. 2024.
items.topic: LUCA and the tree of life

items.head: Synthesis of activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides in prebiotically plausible conditions (Powner, Gerland, Sutherland)
items.who: Powner, Gerland, Sutherland
items.gist: RNA's C and U building blocks made by a route that skips free ribose and free bases, the step that had blocked RNA-world chemistry.
items.plain: Joining a base to ribose sugar, the obvious way to make an RNA letter, does not work for C and U. This team found a side route from simple starting molecules that builds the sugar and base together and ends with an activated nucleotide. Phosphate, though only added into the product at the end, steers several earlier steps.
items.tech: Feedstocks cyanamide, cyanoacetylene, glycolaldehyde, glyceraldehyde and inorganic phosphate; route via arabinose amino-oxazoline and anhydronucleoside intermediates to activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides. Phosphate acts as general acid/base catalyst, nucleophilic catalyst and pH and chemical buffer.
items.borrow: The root of the cyanosulfidic step table. Task #4 records which steps used purified intermediates.

items.head: A production of amino acids under possible primitive Earth conditions (Miller)
items.who: Miller
items.gist: Electric sparks through a mix of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water made amino acids.
items.plain: Stanley Miller circulated gases then thought to make up the early atmosphere, with water, and passed electric sparks through them for a week. Amino acids, building blocks of proteins, appeared. Later work suggests the early atmosphere was less reactive than Miller assumed, but the experiment started laboratory origin-of-life chemistry.
items.tech: Spark discharge through CH4, NH3, H2O and H2 in circulating apparatus; amino acids identified by paper chromatography. Full text not opened (paywalled); details here from the bibliographic record and summaries, so no yields are quoted.
items.borrow: Historical anchor for ladder level L0.

topics: LUCA and the tree of life
